claims.text: Helm is a graduated Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) project.
Helm packages Kubernetes applications as charts, consisting of directories of templated YAML manifests, a `values.yaml` file of default inputs, and metadata.
The `helm` CLI renders chart templates using Go template syntax and either installs the resulting manifests into a cluster as a release or prints them to stdout.
Helm charts are distributed through Helm repositories and indexed publicly on Artifact Hub.
Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0, and the Helm project does not ship a commercial tier.
Pulumi is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
The Pulumi Registry includes providers for AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, Datadog, Cloudflare, GitHub, and Auth0, among others.
Helm manages Kubernetes resources only.
In Pulumi, resource ordering is derived from the dependency graph: each resource waits for its dependencies to become ready, and independent resources deploy in parallel.
Helm applies resources in a fixed order by Kubernetes kind, defined in the Helm source file pkg/release/v1/util/kind_sorter.go.
Helm chart authors cannot declare dependencies between resources or subcharts, except through hook weights.
Helm stores release metadata as Secrets (or ConfigMaps) inside the target Kubernetes cluster.
Pulumi state is managed by Pulumi Cloud by default; self-managed backends include Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, and local files.

Pulumi secrets are encrypted in transit and at rest in the state file by default, with per-stack encryption keys and pluggable KMS providers (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, Google Cloud KMS, HashiCorp Vault).
Helm has no built-in secrets primitive; values typically come from external secret stores or community plugins like helm-secrets.
Pulumi can run via the local CLI, programmatically via Automation API, or remotely in Pulumi Deployments.
A failed Pulumi update leaves the stack in a partially-updated state; `pulumi up` reconciles toward desired state and `pulumi refresh` detects drift.
`helm rollback` restores a Helm release to a previous revision recorded in release history; Helm records each install or upgrade as a numbered release revision.
Pulumi Automation API is a programmatic SDK in every supported Pulumi language for embedding `up`, `preview`, and `destroy` in a host application.
The Helm SDK is available in Go only; other languages must shell out to the `helm` CLI.
Pulumi Packages let a component written in one language be consumed from any other language; Component Resources can be authored in any supported language.
`pulumi import` and the `import` resource option both generate code in the user's language.
Helm has no direct equivalent to import, but existing in-cluster resources can be adopted into a release through resource ownership annotations.
Pulumi Policies are open source, with rules in Python, TypeScript, or Open Policy Agent Rego.
Pulumi Cloud adds centralized policy management, and the Enterprise edition adds Pulumi-maintained policy packs for CIS, PCI DSS, HITRUST, and NIST.
Helm has no native policy engine; policy is typically delegated to Kubernetes admission controllers such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper.

The Helm docs state that "the Kubernetes objects from the charts and all its dependencies are aggregated into a single set; then sorted by type followed by name; and then created/updated in that order."

Helm's kind-sorting order begins with PriorityClasses and Namespaces, then Secrets and ConfigMaps, then CustomResourceDefinitions and RBAC, then Services and workloads, with any kind not on the list (including custom resources) last.
Helm uninstall runs the same kind-sort list in reverse order.
Helm sends the sorted manifests to the API server in a single pass and does not wait for one resource to become ready before applying the next.
Helm chart dependencies do not change ordering: a subchart's objects are merged into the parent chart's set and sorted by kind, so a chart cannot express installing one subchart before another.
Helm chart hooks can be ordered with `helm.sh/hook-weight` annotations, and hook resources are not managed by Helm as part of the release.
Native sequencing for resources and subcharts has been proposed in Helm HIP-0025, which is still a draft.
In Pulumi, passing one resource's output into another, or setting the `dependsOn` resource option, creates an edge in the dependency graph.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider waits for each resource to become ready before creating the resources that depend on it, and deploys independent resources in parallel.
Pulumi deletes resources following the dependency graph in reverse.

`helm.v4.Chart` in the Pulumi Kubernetes provider supports the `config.kubernetes.io/depends-on` annotation for ordering between objects inside the chart, and `dependsOn` on the chart for dependencies on resources outside it.
Pulumi's dependency-graph ordering with parallel deployment of independent resources makes updates both correctly ordered and faster than a strict serial sequence.
Pulumi supports YAML as an authoring language in addition to general-purpose languages.
Pulumi supports HCL as an authoring language in addition to general-purpose languages and YAML.
The Pulumi Registry covers AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and SaaS platforms like Datadog, Auth0, GitHub, and Cloudflare.
Two patterns cover most production deployments of Pulumi and Helm used together.
Helm and Pulumi are commonly used in combination rather than as substitutes.
A Pulumi program can create an EKS, AKS, or GKE cluster and install cert-manager, ingress-nginx, and external-dns through `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release`.
The Pulumi EKS guide walks through the pattern of creating a cluster and installing the operational stack via Helm charts end-to-end.
Pulumi resource outputs flow into a chart's `values` input as typed Pulumi outputs; Pulumi resolves the values at deploy time and orders the chart install after its dependencies.
The FAQ contains an entry titled "What's the difference between `helm.Chart` and `helm.Release`?" that the anchor #whats-the-difference-between-helmchart-and-helmrelease links to.
Pulumi creates and deletes resources in dependency order, with each resource ready before the ones that depend on it, rather than in a fixed order by kind.
There are three common ways to adopt Pulumi alongside or in place of Helm.
Using Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program via `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release` is the most common adoption pattern.
Charts can be converted to native Pulumi code by rendering them with `helm template` and converting the YAML with `pulumi convert --from kubernetes`.
`pulumi import` and the `import` resource option bring existing in-cluster resources under Pulumi management and generate the corresponding code.

The Pulumi Kubernetes provider exposes Helm charts as first-class resources through `helm.v4.Chart` and `helm.v3.Release`, and a Pulumi program can pull charts from any Helm repository (public or private).

`helm.v4.Chart` renders chart templates locally and registers each Kubernetes object the chart produces as an individual Pulumi resource, so every child shows up in plan output, drift detection, and state.
`helm.v3.Release` uses the embedded Helm SDK and creates a real Helm release in the cluster, preserving Helm-specific behaviors like chart hooks, post-rendering, and release history.

Helm merges the objects from a chart and all of its dependencies into a single set, sorts them by Kubernetes kind, and applies them in that order, so declaring a subchart as a dependency does not make it install first.
Ordering within a Helm release requires chart hooks with hook weights or logic in the application itself.
Pulumi can replace Helm: teams can keep installing upstream charts from inside a Pulumi program or move off Helm entirely by converting charts to native Pulumi code.
The Pulumi chart `values` input accepts the same shape as a `values.yaml` file but lets each leaf be a Pulumi output.
